lines.content: description: Write and review Git commit messages using the SE-EDU Git conventions for this project.
Apply these rules whenever proposing or creating a commit:
- Write the subject in imperative mood and capitalize its first letter.
- Do not end the subject with a period.
- Prefer at most 50 characters for the subject; never exceed 72 characters.
- For non-trivial changes, separate the body from the subject with a blank line and wrap body lines at 72 characters.
- Explain what changed and why it was needed; leave implementation details to the diff.
- Split unrelated changes into separate commits.
Use lightweight tags unless the user explicitly requests annotated tags.
description: Apply the SE-EDU Java basic and intermediate coding standard to Java changes in this project.
Apply these rules whenever creating, changing, or reviewing Java code in this repository:
- Use lowercase package names, PascalCase type names, camelCase method and variable names, and SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE constants.
- Use four spaces for indentation, K&R braces, explicit imports, and a hard line limit of 120 characters.
- Keep declarations in the smallest useful scope and use plural names for collections.
- Name boolean values and methods with prefixes such as `is`, `has`, or `can` where practical.
- Put every class in a package and always use braces for loop and conditional bodies.
- Add descriptive Javadocs to public classes and public methods, except trivial accessors, test methods, and exact overrides.
- Use `featureUnderTest_testScenario_expectedBehavior` for test method names when a descriptive name needs multiple parts.
For cases not summarized here, follow the SE-EDU Java basic and intermediate standard, then Google Java Style for uncovered topics.
description: Run Clarry's console UI test cases from test/ui-test-plan.md and compare each transcript with its expected output.
Use this project-specific skill after changing Java code that can affect Clarry's console behaviour.
1. Read `test/ui-test-plan.md`. Each test case contains an aim, an `Inputs` text block, and an `Expected output` text block.
2. Confirm Java 25 is active, then compile all files in `src/main/java` into the ignored `out` directory.
3. Run each test case as a separate Clarry session. Pass the input lines in the order listed, and capture all console output.
4. Compare the complete captured output with the expected-output block, treating only CRLF-versus-LF line endings as equivalent.

5. After every passing test, show the recorded console input and output. If any test fails, stop immediately and show that test's input, actual output, and expected output. Do not continue to later cases.

Keep the test plan in sync with intended UI behaviour before running it. Do not weaken expected outputs to make a failing implementation pass; first determine whether the code or the documented expectation is wrong.
You can add .gradle (e.g. test.gradle) init scripts to this directory. Each one is executed at the start of the build.

This repository is a starter template for a greenfield Java project used in an introductory software engineering course in an undergraduate computer science program. Students use it as the starting point for their own projects.

Unless the user says otherwise, assume that you are assisting a student working on a project in this repository. If the user identifies themselves as an instructor or another project stakeholder, adapt your response to that role.
* Prior knowledge: Basic Java and OOP concepts.
* IDE and level of expertise: Beginner
* Explain the rationale for significant actions: what you did and why.
* Keep explanations brief but instructive, supporting learning through responsible use of AI. For example:
* When suggesting a Git command, briefly explain what it does.
* Add explanatory Javadoc comments to all classes and to nontrivial methods and fields when their purpose or behavior is not obvious.
* Make generated code as self-explanatory as possible, and include explanatory comments where they improve understanding.
* When faced with a design choice, choose the simplest option that is sufficient for the requirements, while briefly explaining relevant more advanced alternatives.
Ensure that Java 25 is used when running the application or build tasks. On macOS, use `sdk use java 25.0.3.fx-zulu` to switch to Java 25 if needed.

After each Java code update that can affect Clarry's console behaviour, update `test/ui-test-plan.md` if the intended UI output changed, then read and invoke `.codex/skills/test-ui/SKILL.md`. Report the recorded input and output, and stop to investigate if a test fails.
Use lightweight tags unless the user requests an annotated tag.
When proposing or creating a commit message, include enough detail to explain the rationale for the change.
Do not commit or push unless explicitly asked.
Apply `.codex/skills/seedu-java-coding-standard/SKILL.md` to every Java code change.
Apply `.codex/skills/seedu-git-standard/SKILL.md` when proposing or creating commits.
Follow the Java and Git standards referenced by `AGENTS.md`.
Clarry is a simple command-line task manager written in Java. It helps you keep track of todos, deadlines, and events without leaving the terminal.
1. Open IntelliJ IDEA and select **File > Open**.
2. Choose this project folder and import it as a Gradle project when prompted.
3. Configure the project SDK to use **JDK 25** and set the language level to **SDK default**.
4. Open [Clarry.java](src/main/java/clarry/Clarry.java), then click the green arrow beside the `main` method.
The fully qualified main class is `clarry.Clarry`. If IntelliJ reports that it cannot find `Clarry`, open
**Run > Edit Configurations** and set **Main class** to `clarry.Clarry`. Also ensure that the project module is
You should see Clarry's welcome banner in the Run console. Type a command and press Enter. Enter `bye` when you are finished.
| `todo DESCRIPTION` | `todo read book` | Adds a todo task. |
| `deadline DESCRIPTION /by DATE` | `deadline submit assignment /by 2026-09-01` | Adds a task with a deadline. |
| `event DESCRIPTION /from START /to END` | `event meeting /from 2026-09-01 14:00 /to 2026-09-01 16:00` | Adds an event. |
| `find KEYWORD` | `find book` | Finds tasks containing a keyword, ignoring letter case. |
| `on DATE` | `on 2026-09-01` | Shows deadlines and events occurring on a date. |
| `mark NUMBER` | `mark 2` | Marks a task as complete. |
| `unmark NUMBER` | `unmark 2` | Marks a task as incomplete. |
Task numbers shown by `list` start at 1.
Dates use `yyyy-MM-dd`, while event date-times use `yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm`.

Clarry automatically saves tasks after every change in `data/clarry.txt` and reloads them next time it starts. The `data` folder is created automatically when needed and is intentionally not tracked by Git, so your personal task list will not be committed to the project.
If the save file is missing, Clarry starts with an empty list. If one saved line is malformed, Clarry skips that line and loads the remaining valid tasks.
